source_metadata.title: New drugs for the management of tuberculosis
source_metadata.author: Gail B. Cross

atoms.canonical_statement: The review aims to summarize recent and emerging advances in tuberculosis treatment, including new therapeutics, repurposed agents, and shortened regimens, and to assess their clinical implications.
The review identifies Nix-TB, ZeNix, TB-PRACTECAL, STREAM, Study 31/A5349, SHINE, TRUNCATE-TB, endTB, and BEAT-TB as landmark trials supporting newer tuberculosis treatment strategies.
The author concludes that newer tuberculosis regimens can reduce treatment burden and adverse effects, but further optimization of combinations, dosing, safety, and access is needed.
The review reports an estimated 10.8 million new tuberculosis cases and 1.3 million deaths in 2023.
Bedaquiline inhibits Mycobacterium tuberculosis ATP synthase while sparing the human counterpart and is active against replicating and nonreplicating bacilli.
The review describes bedaquiline as a cornerstone of rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis treatment.
The review identifies emerging bedaquiline resistance as a major concern that may worsen as global use expands.
The review attributes an important mechanism of bedaquiline resistance to Rv0678 mutations affecting the MmpL5-MmpS5 efflux system and notes cross-resistance concerns related to clofazimine exposure.
The review reports that treatment outcomes for bedaquiline-resistant tuberculosis are poor.

Delamanid and pretomanid are nitroimidazole prodrugs activated by the Mycobacterium tuberculosis enzyme Ddn and exert antimycobacterial effects through mycolic-acid inhibition and respiratory poisoning.

The review reports that combined bedaquiline and delamanid has been associated with a mean QT increase of up to about 20 milliseconds and that clinically significant QT effects generally appear during the first six months and resolve after discontinuation.
Pretomanid and bedaquiline are presented as central components of shortened all-oral BPaLM and BPaL regimens for drug-resistant tuberculosis.

The review reports that newer bedaquiline-based regimens without pretomanid or delamanid have achieved noninferior outcomes in endTB, raising questions about the incremental value of nitroimidazoles in some bedaquiline-containing regimens.

The review describes early bactericidal activity trials as short studies, commonly over the first 14 days, that quantify decline in viable sputum bacilli to screen new tuberculosis drugs and combinations.
TBAJ-876 is described as a next-generation diarylquinoline with increased in-vitro activity, including against Rv0678-mutant strains, and lower predicted QT-prolongation liability than bedaquiline.
Results from the NC-009 Phase 2 evaluation of TBAJ-876 were not yet in the public domain at the time of the review.
Sudapyridine (WX-081) is described as a diarylpyridine related to bedaquiline with preclinical mycobactericidal activity comparable to bedaquiline.
The review reports that sudapyridine had advanced to a Phase 3 trial for rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis.
DprE1 inhibitors target an enzyme required for mycobacterial cell-wall component synthesis, and the review notes that DprE1 has no known human homologue.

A published early bactericidal activity trial of quabodepistat with bedaquiline and delamanid is reported to have shown bactericidal activity comparable to standard RHZE with acceptable safety and tolerability.

Preliminary Phase 2b/c data for quabodepistat, bedaquiline, and delamanid are reported to show end-of-treatment culture conversion comparable to six-month HRZE, with no serious treatment-emergent adverse events reported.
BTZ-043 is reported to penetrate and accumulate in necrotic tuberculosis lesions, a distribution property the review considers favorable for sterilizing difficult-to-reach sites.
A Phase 1/2a trial of BTZ-043 is reported to have shown promising early bactericidal activity and an acceptable safety profile, with mostly mild adverse events.
The review warns that Rv0678-mediated acquired resistance may affect DprE1 inhibitors as well as bedaquiline and clofazimine, creating potential cross-resistance concerns for combination regimens.

Gabfeborole (GSK-656) is reported to have dose-dependent early bactericidal activity with an acceptable pharmacokinetic and safety profile; the review identifies 30 mg as a potentially favorable dose based on bacterial and PET-CT responses.

Telacebec targets the mycobacterial cytochrome bc1aa3 respiratory complex, but Mycobacterium tuberculosis can reroute respiration through cytochrome bd oxidase, reducing telacebec activity to bacteriostatic.

The review reports that daily telacebec doses of 100 to 300 mg were safe and well tolerated in a Phase 2 early bactericidal activity study and produced dose-dependent reductions in sputum mycobacterial load.
The review notes uncertainty about further tuberculosis development of telacebec because alternative respiratory pathways may reduce its antitubercular potency.

In the 76-participant DECODE study, the review reports that delpazolid 1200 mg produced the greatest additive efficacy, whereas 800 mg twice daily was associated with two drug-related serious adverse events in participants with relatively high exposure.
The review reports that sutezolid 600 mg twice daily produced the greatest sputum Mycobacterium tuberculosis clearance in SUDOCU, with no peripheral neuropathy reported during 12 weeks of treatment.
A Phase 2b/c regimen containing quabodepistat, sutezolid, bedaquiline, and a nitroimidazole was terminated after failing to identify a regimen capable of curing tuberculosis in three months or less.
The Nix-TB trial is described as establishing the role of linezolid in highly drug-resistant tuberculosis, with high treatment success but substantial linezolid-associated toxicity.
The ZeNix trial is reported to show that reducing linezolid dose and duration improved safety while maintaining high efficacy.
The review identifies bone marrow suppression, peripheral neuropathy, optic neuropathy, and QT prolongation as important toxicities that can limit sustained linezolid use.

The review suggests that starting linezolid at 600 mg daily for approximately 3 to 4 months followed by a planned reduction to 300 mg may balance efficacy and toxicity in contemporary drug-resistant tuberculosis regimens.
Clofazimine is described as a repurposed component of several pivotal tuberculosis trials, including STREAM, TB-PRACTECAL, TRUNCATE-TB, endTB, and BEAT-TB.

The review notes that clofazimine causes skin discoloration in nearly all recipients with prolonged use and that combination-regimen studies make its independent efficacy contribution difficult to isolate.

Alpibectir is described as enhancing ethionamide bioactivation; the review reports that lower-dose ethionamide plus alpibectir showed early bactericidal activity comparable to isoniazid in a proof-of-concept study.
Earlier four-month fluoroquinolone-containing regimens for drug-susceptible tuberculosis accelerated culture conversion but were associated with higher relapse rates.
Study 31/A5349 is reported to have demonstrated noninferiority of a four-month regimen containing rifapentine 1200 mg and moxifloxacin for drug-susceptible tuberculosis.
The review reports that sitafloxacin showed greater bactericidal activity than levofloxacin in a single early bactericidal activity study without treatment-emergent adverse events.
Meropenem combined with clavulanate is reported to have bactericidal activity against susceptible, resistant, and anaerobic Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
The review identifies intravenous administration and the need to pair meropenem with amoxicillin/clavulanate as practical barriers to broader carbapenem use for tuberculosis.

Dose-escalation studies are reported to show dose-dependent Mycobacterium tuberculosis killing with rifampicin doses up to 35 mg/kg, but recent trials have not reliably shown treatment shortening for drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis.
The review notes emerging evidence that higher rifampicin doses may be less well tolerated.
For central nervous system tuberculosis, the review states that standard rifampicin 10 mg/kg often produces undetectable cerebrospinal-fluid concentrations and may be inadequate.

The review reports that rifampicin 20 mg/kg intravenously or 35 mg/kg orally can achieve cerebrospinal-fluid concentrations above the rifampicin MIC in most participants with acceptable safety in studied regimens.
Preliminary ESCMID 2025 findings are reported to suggest that rifampicin 35 mg/kg did not reduce mortality in tuberculous meningitis and increased hepatotoxicity.
The review attributes part of Study 31 success to rifapentine pharmacokinetics, noting a longer plasma half-life than rifampicin and use of rifapentine 1200 mg in the four-month regimen.
The review notes emerging real-world evidence that the four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen may be less well tolerated than expected, with intolerance driven mainly by the rifamycin.

Study 31 was the first cited trial in the review to successfully shorten standard drug-susceptible tuberculosis treatment to four months, including among people living with HIV with CD4 counts at least 100 cells per microliter.
The review states that the four-month rifapentine-moxifloxacin regimen from Study 31 has been incorporated into WHO treatment guidance.
Post-hoc analyses are described as linking success of shorter tuberculosis regimens to baseline disease burden and achieved drug exposure.

TRUNCATE-TB is reported to show that many patients with drug-susceptible pulmonary tuberculosis can be treated with a two-month strategy using bedaquiline, linezolid, isoniazid, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol when relapse is managed with close monitoring and retreatment.
TB-PRACTECAL is reported to show that a six-month BPaLM regimen was more effective and safer than conventional longer treatment for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis.

The review reports that endTB and BEAT-TB provide additional evidence that shorter multidrug-resistant tuberculosis regimens built around bedaquiline, linezolid, a fluoroquinolone, and pyrazinamide, with or without another companion drug, can be highly effective.

The SHINE trial is reported to demonstrate that four months of standard treatment was as effective as six months for children with nonsevere, smear-negative, drug-susceptible tuberculosis and reduced treatment burden.

PredictTB is reported to have found relapse or treatment failure in 12% of participants treated with four months of RHZE versus 1.5% with six months, despite selecting patients with low disease burden.

Synthesizing PredictTB, TRUNCATE-TB, Study 31, and SHINE, the review concludes that four-month treatment with standard drugs is unlikely to succeed outside low-burden, noncavitary disease and that more potent agents may be required for broader treatment shortening.

The review proposes a precision-medicine direction for tuberculosis that may incorporate therapeutic drug monitoring, immune endotypes, multiplex biomarkers, and risk-adapted treatment duration or drug selection.
The review cautions that increasingly complex precision-treatment strategies will require implementation science from the outset to remain usable in resource-limited tuberculosis programs.

The review describes adaptive and platform trials as flexible infrastructures that can evaluate multiple tuberculosis drugs and treatment strategies concurrently and highlights TBTC, UNITE4TB, and SMART4TB as examples.

The review concludes that scientific advances in tuberculosis therapeutics must be paired with equitable drug access, person-centred support, stronger health systems, and implementation science to translate shorter and safer regimens into population benefit.
The author reports support from the Burnet Institute.
The author reports no conflicts of interest.

extraction_limitations: The governing LiteratureAtom model is designed for primary literature, whereas this source is a narrative review.
Atoms represent assertions made by the review. Trial findings cited by the review are tagged secondary_reported_result and must not be treated as primary-study atoms.
The review does not report a systematic search strategy, formal study-selection criteria, or study-level risk-of-bias assessment.
Some pipeline claims rely on conference presentations, trial registries, or unpublished/preliminary results available at the time of review.
No missing study-level denominators, effect estimates, or participant details were invented.
